analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license and registration for every handgun in states without a comparable system.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Attorney General to create a federal handgun licensing and registration system. Anyone who owns or carries a handgun would need a license—requiring a background check, fingerprints, a photo, and firearms safety training—and would have to register each handgun with law enforcement. States that already run a licensing and registration system meeting the bill's standards, like states with handgun purchase permits, could be certified to keep their own system instead. The bill also authorizes federal grants to help states, local governments, and tribes build these systems, and gives states two years after enactment before the rules take effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that do not already license and register handguns, especially communities most affected by gun violence, would gain a system meant to keep handguns away from people prohibited from having them and to give police a record of every handgun's owner. Law enforcement agencies would gain access to registration records for tracing guns used in crimes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states without handgun licensing

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful to own, possess, or control a handgun without both a license and a registered weapon, with license eligibility barred for people under 21, non-citizens without permanent status, people who have not completed safety training, and anyone federally prohibited from possessing firearms.
The federal system must include a method for easily retrieving information identifying each handgun owner and each handgun, giving law enforcement a registry for tracing.

States can keep their own system if the Attorney General certifies it meets the same standards, including criminal penalties for unlicensed, unregistered possession and for unlicensed ammunition transfers; the certification is revoked if the state's system falls short.

The bill authorizes competitive grants to states, local governments, and Indian tribes to build or comply with licensing and registration systems, subject to audits every two years and an annual report to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Handgun owners would pay licensing costs and bear the burden of fingerprints, photos, safety training, and registration for each handgun; anyone caught with an unlicensed or unregistered handgun would face fines and mandatory imprisonment that a court cannot suspend. Firearms dealers and manufacturers would face a market where every handgun transfer runs through a licensed, registered framework. Taxpayers would fund the federal system and the state implementation grants, which are authorized at unspecified sums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun owners, firearms dealers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes criminal penalties on unlicensed possession, and any sentence of imprisonment imposed cannot be suspended by the court, meaning a lawful owner who misses a step in the process could face mandatory jail time.

The license requirements—fingerprints, a recent face photograph, safety training, and registration of each weapon—place a standing burden on every handgun owner in covered states, and license holders must renew at least every five years.

The bill takes effect only two years after enactment and leaves implementation details largely to Attorney General regulations, so the actual rules gun owners would face depend heavily on future executive action.
Licensing and registration schemes face sustained constitutional and political opposition from gun rights advocates, which is a principal reason this bill had no realistic path in the 115th Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's public-safety goal—a verifiable record of who owns which handgun, with licenses denied to prohibited people—is real, and the state certification and grant provisions give states flexibility and funding. But it is written broadly: it treats unlicensed possession of a single handgun as a crime with mandatory, non-suspendable imprisonment, and it places fingerprinting, photographing, training, and registration requirements on every lawful owner. The costs fall hardest on the estimated tens of millions of existing handgun owners in the roughly forty-plus states without comparable licensing systems, and the design leaves a great deal to Attorney General discretion. Supporters would call that a fair price for traceability; critics would call it a de facto restriction on gun ownership.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which passed it along to its crime subcommittee, where it sat until the two-year Congress ended—no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on April 24, 2018, joined by eight original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
On May 22, 2018, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations.
No further action was taken, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill ever receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The firearms industry and gun owners opposed to licensing and registration are better off, since no licensing or registration requirement was ever enacted. Congressional supporters of gun regulation got nothing from the effort beyond a recorded position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms industry and unlicensed gun owners

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Handgun Licensing and Registration Act and assembled eight original cosponsors.

for.name: Nine Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Pallone, Sires, Espaillat, Chu, Norton, Wasserman Schultz, and Wilson.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chairman and majority of the House Judiciary Committee (115th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and House majority floor managers
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor agenda and never brought the bill up for a vote.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal handgun licensing and registration proposals and lobbied congressional Republicans against them.

sides.party_line_note: All ten backers—the sponsor and nine cosponsors—were Democrats, and gun licensing legislation in this era drew essentially no Republican support; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: A licensing-and-registration requirement would add compliance steps to every handgun transaction and could shrink the market by making ownership harder in most states. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the bill's public-safety aim.

Current owners would face new licensing, fingerprinting, photo, training, and registration requirements—and criminal penalties with non-suspendable jail time for noncompliance. Owners who keep and use handguns lawfully would bear most of the bill's direct costs.
